analysis.one_liner: Removes the federal 30-day notice requirement before evicting renters in federally backed housing.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote, so renters in federally backed housing keep the 30-day eviction notice protection.
analysis.plain_summary: The CARES Act gave renters in federally assisted or federally backed housing — for example, apartments whose mortgages are guaranteed by federal agencies — a guaranteed 30 days' notice before a landlord can start an eviction. This bill would delete that federal requirement, leaving eviction notice rules entirely to each state. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, received no hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Landlords and property owners of federally assisted or federally backed rental housing. They could start eviction proceedings sooner, without waiting out a federal 30-day notice, and would rely only on their state's notice rules. Owners of large federally financed apartment portfolios would have the most to gain, since the federal rule applies to them nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Landlords of federally backed rental housing

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the CARES Act requirement that landlords give tenants in federally assisted or federally backed housing a 30-day notice before beginning eviction proceedings.
As the title suggests, it leaves eviction notice periods entirely to state housing laws, so a landlord would follow only state deadlines instead of a uniform federal one.
The bill was introduced by Rep. Barry Loudermilk with 9 cosponsors (8 Republicans and 1 Democrat).

analysis.who_pays: Renters living in federally assisted or federally backed housing would lose their guaranteed 30-day notice and could face an eviction filing sooner, leaving less time to find new housing, gather rent, or respond before a case starts in court.

drawbacks.text: Renters in covered housing would lose the guaranteed 30-day buffer before an eviction begins, which is the time they need to pay arrears, find a new place, or prepare a defense. The CRS summary and bill text confirm the provision strikes that notice requirement outright rather than reforming it.

The strongest good-faith objection from supporters' side: in many states the federal 30-day notice duplicates a similar state-law notice, so landlords in those states face two overlapping notice rules for the same eviction, adding delay to cases where the tenant is not paying rent.

Because the federal rule applies to properties with federally backed mortgages across all 50 states, repealing it would also strip the notice in states whose own laws give less protection than 30 days.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to landlords is real but modest: faster paperwork in states that already have their own notice rules. The cost falls on a narrow but vulnerable group — renters in federally financed housing — who would lose a uniform 30-day cushion in the states with the weakest tenant protections. The trade tilts toward property owners, and the bill offered nothing to tenants in return.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Barry Loudermilk introduced the bill on September 29, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee markup, and no vote in either chamber before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill drew 9 cosponsors (8 Republicans and 1 Democrat), a small base of support that did not push it past referral.
Because the bill never became law, the CARES Act's 30-day notice requirement in federally assisted and federally backed housing remains in force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters in federally assisted and federally backed housing are better off, since the 30-day notice requirement stayed on the books; landlords of those properties did not get the faster eviction timeline they sought.

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the CARES Act's 30-day pre-eviction notice requirement.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was almost entirely Republican — 8 of its 9 cosponsors — and it never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would have shown a fuller partisan split.

industries.industry: Residential landlords (owners of federally assisted or federally backed rental properties)
industries.note: The bill would have let these landlords start evictions without the federal 30-day notice, shortening the runway for tenants facing eviction. The gain comes directly out of tenants' time to respond, so the industry's interest runs against renters in covered housing.
Firms managing federally financed apartment portfolios would face one less federal compliance step in eviction filings. As with owners, the time saved comes from the tenant's notice period.
